description: Que niños y niñas de 7 a 12 años vivan en primera persona cómo funciona una misión espacial a la Luna o a Marte. Lo hacen mediante un juego de supervivencia y simulación basado en datos reales de la NASA. Así descubren qué recursos son vitales para terminarla con éxito (energía, aire, comida, protección contra la radiación y el bienestar de la tripulación) y que cada decisión tiene un costo.
summary: Children aged 7 to 12 can experience firsthand how a space mission to the Moon or Mars works. They do this through a survival and simulation game based on real NASA data. In the process, they discover which resources are vital for a successful mission—such as energy, air, food, radiation protection, and the well-being of the crew—and learn that every decision comes at a cost.
details: Orbit Junior is a survival game for kids aged 7 to 12 that runs in the browser, in Spanish and English, with nothing to install. Carlos Martínez, an astronaut from the (fictional) Argentine Space Agency, is stranded at the Moon's south pole after a micrometeorite damages his spacecraft and his oxygen generator, and the player has 14 days to help him get back home. Players explore the base in first person, in a pixel art graphic adventure, and each day they decide which systems to power with the scarce energy from the solar panels and which task Carlos does: collect ice, repair the ship, gather samples or rest. No option is free. The game's solar storms are real flares recorded by NASA DONKI and fetched live, the events show real studies from NASA OSDR, the ending uses the latest photo of Earth taken by the EPIC camera, and at the end a summary shows which decision led to each outcome. The game teaches through experience how a space mission is managed: limited resources, priorities, the effects of space weather and the importance of communications. It also brings authentic scientific data to a young audience and can be used in schools to spark interest in science and critical thinking, because winning depends on planning and understanding the consequences of each decision, not on luck. We built it with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Canvas for the pixel art animated effects (sparks, alarms, shooting stars, the meteorite flash and the reactions of the hidden surprises); the Web Audio API for the 8-bit music and sound effects generated in the browser; NASA APIs (DONKI, EPIC and OSDR); a Node.js script that saves a copy of the OSDR and DONKI data, because OSDR cannot be queried from the browser; and AI-generated pixel art processed with Python. It is creative because it turns real scientific data into game mechanics, so each playthrough changes based on what the Sun actually did, and it combines this with a comic-strip intro, illustrated endings and hidden surprises that reward exploration. We took into account the age of the audience (short texts, icons, a guided tutorial and endings where no one dies), scientific accuracy (it shows where the data comes from) and and custom icons that display on any device).
